accuracy.reason: All eight objectives are accurate at overview scope: persistent managed operations and recovery limits; requirements before labels; six layouts and access mechanisms; overlapping capabilities; read/write/storage/operating costs; and the partition-specific C/A conflict. No SQL/NoSQL or extension-based guarantee. Sources support the claims, with primary followups needed for broad overview links.

evidence.quote: Categories describe common strengths, not exclusive capabilities. A relational database can store JSON; a document database can support transactions. Check the actual product, deployment and operation rather than assuming a category supplies the required guarantee.
An isolated reader cannot learn a completed write from an unreachable copy. Returning old data sacrifices consistency; waiting indefinitely or refusing the affected operation sacrifices availability.

mechanisms.reason: The same-product diagram concretely distinguishes joined tables, a nested document and a key lookup. Specialized diagrams map partition grouping, graph paths and similarity to distinct queries. Index upkeep, duplicated-update work and the isolated reader explain causal costs and failure, sufficient to transfer this overview without demanding implementation algorithms.

evidence.quote: An index is an extra access structure that can locate relevant rows without examining every record for suitable queries. It consumes storage and needs maintenance when data changes.
An isolated reader cannot learn a completed write from an unreachable copy. Returning old data sacrifices consistency; waiting indefinitely or refusing the affected operation sacrifices availability.

coherence.reason: Persistence and requirements precede models; specialized capabilities precede overlap and costs; replication and communication failure are defined before CAP. Each of the eight cards contributes to the final requirements-to-choice argument. Diagrams reinforce the relevant layouts and costs without implying equivalence of guarantees.

evidence.quote: The data model describes how information is organized: tables, documents, keys and values, or connected nodes. An access pattern describes how the application finds, filters, combines or updates that information.
Connect each requirement to a data layout or capability, then name its write, storage, coordination or operating cost. If copies are distributed, explain behavior when they cannot communicate.

decisions.reason: Connects queries and joint correctness rules to layouts, indexes and costs; existing extensions may avoid another system, while measured operating limits can justify one. Recovery, staleness and partition behavior enter the choice. The last card makes changed workloads and measurements grounds for reconsideration.

evidence.quote: Keeping these tasks together can reduce the number of systems to run. A separate service can still make sense when workload needs or operating limits justify it. Measure those needs instead of assuming one store must do everything.
Measure representative queries and updates. Changed access patterns, traffic or recovery requirements can change the choice; popularity and product names are not substitutes for this reasoning.

clarity.reason: Terms are defined before consequential use, including the two meanings of partition. Compact layout diagrams help. The six-model survey and generic decision checklist remain dense for a beginner, especially the combined wide-column/graph/vector card, but every required distinction is explainable from the text.

evidence.quote: In Cassandra-style layouts, a partition key groups records for targeted access. Design that grouping around known queries. Poor keys can overload a partition; a new query may need a new table. This data partition is distinct from a network partition, which is a communication failure.

An embedding represents an item as a list of numbers. Similarity search finds nearby vectors under a chosen measure; it can support retrieval by meaning. Approximate search trades some result accuracy for speed. Similarity does not prove exact equality or factual correctness.

outcomes.reason: Actual learner covers managed persistent data, layout-dependent queries/updates/rules, recovery configuration and backups, entities/relationships/access, growth/latency/operating constraints, and product/deployment-specific guarantees. All quoted evidence is exact and entails these claims.

Explains relational rows/columns/joins/constraints; document grouping and duplicate-update cost; known-key access limits; Cassandra query-oriented partition grouping distinct from network failure; graph traversal; and metric-based vector similarity with approximation and truth/equality limits. All six criteria are taught and supported; algorithm details are correctly left unspecified.

Uses PostGIS and pgvector to establish overlap without performance equivalence; requires measurement, names extra-store synchronization/operating costs, index structure/storage/upkeep, duplicate-read versus update coordination, and remote communication/partial failures. Potential copy disagreement follows the coordination teaching rather than an invented guarantee.

Defines replicas and live-but-disconnected nodes, distinguishes formal C/A, derives missing-information conflict, scopes it to affected operations/configurations, and connects requirements to concrete cost categories, recovery, measurements and reassessment. No vendor or multiple-store prescription is needed. Exact evidence supports every criterion.

sourceChecks.claim: Tutorial establishes relational managed records; persistence/recovery limits additionally checked against PostgreSQL backup-file documentation. Migration and recovery advice is bounded engineering reasoning, not a claimed vendor guarantee.

PostgreSQL JSON page establishes category overlap; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/transactions/ confirms document-store transactions with configuration qualifications. Requirements are selection guidance, not a benchmark.

MongoDB modeling supports access-oriented document structure; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/best-practices/ explicitly explains embedding/reference and duplicate-update costs. PostgreSQL tutorial supports rows/columns; layout diagram preserves the same product with differing access work.

Cassandra logical modeling supports query-driven partition grouping and table-per-query; graph concepts verified at https://neo4j.com/docs/getting-started/appendix/graphdb-concepts/ and vector metrics/approximate recall tradeoff at https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector. Similarity is correctly limited to a representation and measure.

Documentation landing page is an index; https://postgis.net/ confirms spatial storage/index/query features, and https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector confirms PostgreSQL vector extension. Attempted manual-3.6 page was inaccessible, so feature verification uses accessible project primary pages. No equal-performance claim.

Index introduction verifies selective access and maintenance overhead; MongoDB best-practices primary followup supports duplicate-data read/update tradeoff. Distribution and extra-store costs follow from remote copies and independent recovery responsibilities, without numeric performance guarantees.

FoundationDB CAP explanation confirms disconnected live replicas cannot share writes and distinguishes all-node formal availability from service availability. Slide accurately avoids importing the source page’s broad ACID slogan into a universal category claim.

Same tutorial confirms relational structure, not a product-ranking algorithm. Requirements-first recommendation is a synthesis of the checked model, index, replication, extension and recovery sources; no empirical result or universal winner asserted.
